parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Bishop's Opening
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 at once, eyeing f7 and discouraging ...d5, while keeping the f-pawn free for f4 and delaying the knight on g1. Unlike the Italian, White does not commit a knight to f3 on move two, so the opening is highly transpositional: after 2...Nc6 it tends to become an Italian or Vienna, after 2...Nf6 White usually plays 3.d3 (or the sharp Urusov Gambit 3.d4), and after 2...Bc5 play is symmetrical and can reach a Giuoco Piano. Theory judges it equal with best play. At master level it is a surprise weapon used to avoid Petrov preparation, not a main line.

parent.name: English Opening
parent.overview: White opens with the c-pawn to contest d5 from the wing, keeping the e4, d4, g3 and b3 options open until Black reveals a set-up. It is a flexible, hypermodern, mostly positional opening: not as sharp as 1.e4 or 1.d4, with the character decided by Black's reply and by transpositions into the Queen's Gambit, Réti or King's Indian. Principal branches are the Reversed Sicilian (1...e5, with an extra tempo for White), the Symmetrical (1...c5, often with a Maroczy bind) and the Anglo-Indian (1...Nf6 and 1...e6/...g6 transpositions). White typically plays Nc3, g3 and Bg2, and expands on the queenside with Rb1 and b4, or takes the classical centre with e4. The database root is a crossroads; its most-played continuations are transpositions to QGD (1.c4 e6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d4), the King's Indian and the Réti.

parent.name: Philidor Defense
parent.overview: Black defends e5 with the d-pawn instead of the knight, building a compact centre at the cost of space and piece mobility. Wikipedia calls it solid but passive (s1); the dark-squared bishop and sometimes the whole position can be cramped (s2, s4). The usual game is White taking space after 3.d4 or developing with 3.Bc4, and Black setting up the Hanham formation (...Nf6, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...c6, ...O-O), then freeing the position by ...exd4 or ...d5 at the right moment (s1, s4). Modern analysis finds it dynamically balanced, not just passive (s3). Strong players use it rarely; Wikipedia says no top player used it regularly as of 2017, though it has grown in rapid, blitz and bullet (s1). Move orders matter: Black must avoid several tactical pitfalls (s2, s4).

parent.name: Englund Gambit
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...e5, offering the e-pawn after 2.dxe5 to avoid closed queen's-pawn positions and set tactical problems. The main line is 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Nc3, where Black regains the pawn on b2 but loses the queenside attack; the gambit relies on traps such as 6.Bc3?? Bb4! with mate threats on c1. White can simply keep the pawn and, with accurate development, retains an advantage. Strong players and engines consider it unsound for Black, and top-level players almost never choose it. It scores through quick development and traps against an unprepared opponent.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
parent.overview: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 is a crossroads, not one system: White develops the b1-knight before committing the c-pawn, which blocks White's own c-pawn and so gives up the usual c4 challenge to d5. The usual continuation is 2...Nf6, after which White chooses between 3.Bg5 (Richter-Veresov: pin on f6, queenside castling, f3 and e4) and 3.Bf4 (Jobava London: Nb5 ideas against c7, Qd2 and Bh6 against a fianchetto), or 3.Nf3 and transpositions. Other Black replies are 2...Bf5 (Alburt Defence, assessed as equal, rare in master play), 2...c5 (Irish Gambit, little explored) and 2...e6. The openings are rarely used by top players as a main weapon but are sound; Spassky, Tal, Karpov, Bronstein, Morozevich, Aronian and Gashimov have played them as surprise weapons. The subtree also swallows a different opening by transposition: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6 is the Chigorin Defence, Black's choice, not White's.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense
parent.overview: Black fianchettoes the dark-squared bishop, castles and lets White build a big pawn centre (c4, d4, e4), then attacks it with ...e5 or ...c5 while preparing kingside play. In the main Classical/Mar del Plata structure the centre locks after d5 and the game becomes a race: White expands on the queenside with c4-c5 while Black storms the kingside with ...f5-f4 and ...g5. Other White systems change the picture: Samisch (f3) is aggressive with opposite-side castling attacks, Four Pawns (f4) maximises space, Averbakh (Bg5) keeps ...e5 in check, and the Fianchetto (g3) is quieter and positional. Sources describe it as dynamic, exceptionally complex and moderately risky for both sides, with a heavy theory burden because White has many fifth-move systems. Considered sound today after being held suspect until the 1930s.

parent.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5
parent.overview: Both sides develop the king's bishop to its active diagonal (Bc4 and ...Bc5), eyeing f7/f2. White's choice at move 4 decides the character. Slow lines are 4.c3 followed by d3 or d4 and the modern Giuoco Pianissimo with d3 (Re1, Nbd2-f1-g3, a4, h3): White postpones any central clash and the game is a patient manoeuvring battle. The sharper lines are the classical 4.c3 Nf6 5.d4 (Greco's Attack, Moller Attack), where White sacrifices a pawn for initiative, and the Evans Gambit 4.b4, a pawn for rapid development and an attack on f7. The Three Knights 4.Nc3 and 4.O-O are also main subtree moves. Black mirrors development, challenges the centre with ...d5, and has sufficient defensive resources. It is a respected choice used by Karpov and, as a Ruy Lopez sidestep, by Carlsen.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Closed
parent.overview: White declines the Open Sicilian by playing 2.Nc3, keeping d5 covered and delaying d4. The usual plan is a slow kingside build-up with g3, Bg2, d3, Be3 and f4, aiming at f4-f5 and an attack on the black king, with d4 kept as an option. Black develops (...Nc6, ...g6, ...Bg7, ...d6, ...e6 are all common) and looks for queenside counterplay, typically ...b5 and a rook on the c- or b-file, before White's attack arrives. Spassky played it aggressively with an early f4 and Nf3; Smyslov was calmer, with Be3, Qd2 and Nge2. The line 3.f4 (Grand Prix Attack) is a more direct, sharper cousin. Overall it is a low-theory, plans-driven opening in which both sides race on opposite wings.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.
